app.title: SEM analyzer: measure features on micrographs and assemble figure panels
app.summary: A person loads a folder or upload of electron micrographs, along with any instrument metadata files, and picks one from a thumbnail sidebar. They set the scale, either automatically from the metadata and the detected scale bar or by drawing a line over the scale bar and typing its length. Then they draw lines and circles on the image, and each one becomes a length or diameter in real units, written on the image and added to a table. They can crop the instrument info strip, add a clean scale bar, a panel label and text boxes, and download the annotated PNG and a measurement CSV. They can also pick several images in order and lay them out as one labelled figure with scale bars, which downloads as a PNG or as a ZIP of the processed images.

task.text: Measure lengths and diameters of features in calibrated micrographs, and prepare the annotated images and multi-panel figures for publication.

data.text: A set of microscope images, each with an optional key=value metadata file giving magnification and scale-bar length, plus the table of measurements drawn on each image.
data.item: a single micrograph with its calibration and the shapes drawn on it

stage.text: measuring features on micrographs after imaging, and preparing figures for a paper

mechanism.text: A sidebar of thumbnails chooses the image open in the main view. There, a drawing canvas turns each line or circle into a calibrated length that is written on the image and gathered in a table, while side controls set the calibration, crop and figure overlays that are composed into the canvas background. A second mode uses the same sidebar to queue images in click order and tiles them into one figure grid with per-panel scale bars and letter labels.

field.text: scale-calibrated measurement of SEM micrographs and figure preparation in materials science

workflow.name: calibrate images to real units, measure features, and assemble a figure

steps.here: A native folder picker or a typed path loads every image in a folder, or several images are uploaded with their matching .txt metadata files. Each image is calibrated automatically where the metadata allows.
Clicking a thumbnail opens that image on the drawing canvas. Each thumbnail shows whether its image is calibrated yet.

steps.step: set the scale from a known reference
steps.here: Auto-calibration divides the metadata's MicronMarker length by the scale-bar length detected in the bottom info strip. Manual calibration means drawing a line over the scale bar and entering its real length in µm.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Lines drawn on the canvas give lengths and circles give diameters in µm or nm. Labels are written along each line, and the values build up in a table. Shapes can be moved, resized or deleted, and Ctrl+Z undoes.

steps.step: add figure annotations to the image
steps.here: Options to crop the info strip, draw a new scale bar with a rounded length, add a corner panel label such as 'a)', and place free text boxes.
Downloads the annotated PNG and a CSV of the measurements, both named after the project and image.

In Figures mode, thumbnails clicked in order are tiled into a grid with a set number of columns, a gap, a background colour and cell width. Each cell is cropped and gets a scale bar and an auto letter label. The result downloads as one PNG or as a ZIP of the processed cells.

distinctive: Each image must be calibrated (µm per pixel) before any measurement shows in real units. The calibration comes from instrument metadata plus automatic detection of a tick-ruler scale bar, or from a hand-drawn line over the bar.
Measured values are drawn onto the image, rotated to run along each line, so the exported picture carries its own measurements.
The instrument's black data strip at the bottom of each image is detected so it can be cropped off before the figure is made.
Scale-bar lengths are rounded to 1, 2 or 5 × 10^n, and montage panels can keep each image's original scale-bar length or use one shared length.
Everything runs locally as a desktop app so unpublished images never leave the machine.
